items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
I used to take my online privacy really seriously, having no social media, not using google or its services, using fake email addresses and fake names, always erasing cookies and site data, all the protections one can take to be tracked as little as possible.

But sharing my life is something that I love, and I don't want it to be private. I find it so awesome that thanks to internet, random people can know what you are doing and who you are.
What I don't like about Instagram and other social medias is that I'm giving my data away for free to big corporations and they can do whatever they want with it.
To put it another way, I'm not scared about someone random knowing where I live and what I like. Rather I'm upset that people are making money over where I live and what I like.

So lately, I caved in. I stopped making all these efforts to protect my online life because they were tiring, isolating and stripping me of something I liked.

items.title: Before improving a system, decide how you’ll measure the result
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
If You Don’t Measure Something, You Can’t Improve It

You’d be surprised how often I’ve found myself in engineering discussions asking how often something occurs and getting a blank stare.

Without any measurement, you are operating on vibes alone.

Engineering teams are always looking to improve something: maybe you want to reduce latency, increase system throughput, reduce production incidents, or make a dent in your pull request queue.
Yet time and time again, I see teams start changing systems without any way to measure the results.
Something might feel faster, or incidents might feel less frequent; but are they?

Before I improve anything, I make sure I can measure it.

Measure to Understand

The first step to improving anything is understanding where you are today.

Take latency as an example.
If you want to improve a system's end-to-end response time, start by measuring it.

How long does a single request take?
What’s the average?
The 90th percentile?

items.title: What Cooperation Does Not Concede
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
One of you glances toward an open window and says, “It’s getting cold in here.” Your housemate closes it. Both know what was wanted. Neither has had to announce who is entitled to give the other instructions.

An indirect request can separate agreement to an action from agreement about who may demand it. The literal remark supplies a description both can accept: one person mentioned a problem; the other chose to help. If the window stays open, the remark can be allowed to pass without anyone announcing a refusal. The intention need not be secret for the relationship to remain unspecified.

Direct requests can preserve equality. This advantage of indirection arises when an explicit request risks becoming a test of rank—and when both parties are willing to leave that test unspoken.

Between equal departments, “Would it be possible to have the report today?” may preserve no more autonomy than “Please send the report today.” Both are conventional requests. “The report would help at…

items.title: Going public
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
In August I wrote about how I built Travel Log, a private travel journal for iPhone that builds your travel history by itself. That post ended with two promises, more or less. The first was that I might publish smaller parts of the code at some point. The second was that the App Store release would come “in a few days/weeks.”

The few days/weeks turned into three months. And instead of publishing smaller parts, I published the whole thing.

As of today, Travel Log is on the App Store and its source code is on GitHub under the MIT license.

This comes down to trust. Travel Log keeps a detailed record of where you have been. The entire pitch of the app is that this record stays on your phone: no account, no server of my own, no analytics. Until now, you had to take my word for it.

items.title: Solvej Balle — On the Calculation of Volume, Book V (2026)
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Over the weekend, I read through the fifth instalment in Solvej Balle’s series On The Calculation of Volume, as newly published in English translation. I’ve evangelised for the series a few times here in the past (starting here ), so I’ll keep this brief. It suffices to say that Balle continues to find new ways to keep her time-loop story fresh. Within its constraints, she has probed many spheres of the human experience. This current book turns a lens on questions of society—eg how is it (re-)formed; how does it operate?—and the structures of knowledge: eg how are things known, and how do we categorise what we think or feel or believe alongside that which is provable? 

I remain utterly captivated by Balle’s project and her prose; I’m already counting down to the 6 May release of the penultimate volume. 

Wishing you a happy Tara Selter Day.

Why genuine leadership begins with human connection, and why treating people well should be fundamental to running a successful business.

Almost every large organisation makes some variation of the same statement.

Our people are our greatest asset.

It's a reassuring sentiment. It appears on corporate websites, in annual reports, during leadership presentations and across recruitment campaigns.

But I've often wondered how many businesses genuinely believe it.

Not because I think business leaders are necessarily dishonest, or because organisations deliberately set out to treat employees badly.

But because there often seems to be a significant difference between what companies say about their people and how they actually operate.

items.title: Risk = likelihood x impact
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
This is a simple formula.

It says that the risk associated with a given event increases when either or both the likelihood of this event or the impact (negative or positive) of the same event increase.

So, risk of meatballs falling from the sky is low, because the likelihood of meatballs falling from the sky is low.

But if we were living in a world where meatballs falling from the sky was a common thing, then the risks associated with all possible events should be assessed. Examples of events: losses to the shareholders of the food industry, food poisoning due to eating a meatball fallen two weeks ago... You can make them as serious or stupid as you want.

There's a whole lot of industrious corporate hustlers dealing with inventing and assessing risks of all sorts in exchange for eye watering consulting fees.

Amongst those people the IT security experts.
